$comment: The shared contract: what a client repeats after a failure, and what it answers as is.
A change here is a change to every SDK. Each target reads this file from its own suite, makes
the API answer each case over a real socket and watches whether its own client issues the
request again, so a verdict edited here fails every target that still disagrees with it.
A client reads a failure in this order. A failure that never produced an answer takes the
verdict of its cause under `transport`. An answer whose body names a problem the `problems`
list carries takes that verdict. Any other answer takes the verdict of its status, which is
also what an older client falls back to when the API names a problem it has never heard of.
The `problems` list covers the API's whole problem catalogue, on purpose: a problem added to
the API and left out of here fails the generator's own check until somebody decides whether it
retries. That is the point of the list being exhaustive rather than a list of exceptions.
The same status can carry either verdict, which is why the problem wins over it: the quotas and
the instance pacing below all answer 429, and only pacing clears inside a send's delay budget.
The `transport` causes are the same shape for the same reason. A client that decides by which
of its own error types carries the failure retries a mistyped API URL and a response that broke
its own ceiling as if they were a reset connection: the verdict follows the cause, not the type.
Failures that produced no answer to read, told apart by what caused them rather than by which
type a client happens to wrap them in. Only one of them could end differently, and a client
that groups them together spends four attempts on a wrong URL and then blames the network in
the message it hands its caller.
A target maps each cause onto the failures of its own runtime and provokes it for real: a
socket that hangs up, a body above the ceiling, a URL nothing can be sent to.

causes.reason: a request that got no answer says nothing about whether the API acted on it, and the identifier the client chose is what keeps a second attempt from ingesting the event twice
the answer crossed a ceiling this client set for itself, and the same request draws the same answer; retrying reads the oversized head or body again, four times over
nothing was ever sent, because there is nowhere to send it; a repetition builds the same unusable request, and the retries turn a misconfiguration into a message that accuses the network

$comment: What a client does with the delay the API names beside a retryable answer.
It is the API's estimate of when the request becomes servable, so it is preferred over the
client's own schedule when it can be read. It is also written by the other end, so it is
bounded like anything else that arrives from there: the wait it asks for is cut down to what
is left of the send's delay budget, and a send whose budget is spent stops rather than waits.
retry_after.honoured_when: the answer is one this file classifies as retryable and the header names a whole number of seconds that is not negative
retry_after.bounded_by: max_total_delay_ms, less what the delays of this send have already spent

cases.name: a delay the budget can afford is the one waited out
a delay of no seconds sends the next attempt straight away
a delay far above the budget is cut down to what is left of it
a delay that is not a number of seconds leaves the client's own schedule in place
a delay written as a date leaves the client's own schedule in place
a delay pointing backwards leaves the client's own schedule in place
